Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1238–1251. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.74.5.1238

gentle.headline: Share one sentence with someone you trust about how your week has felt.
gentle.how_to: Focus on the feeling, for example 'Tired but proud of getting through a busy week'.

evidence.summary: Research shows that sharing personal feelings, more than facts alone, is a strong predictor of how close people feel. A one-sentence check-in is an easy start.
evidence.detail_source: Laurenceau 1998. (new practice added to complete the Gentle/Moderate/Deep family)
references: Laurenceau, J.-P., Barrett, L. F., & Pietromonaco, P. R. (1998). Intimacy as an interpersonal process: The importance of self-disclosure, partner disclosure, and perceived partner responsiveness in interpersonal exchanges. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1238–1251. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.74.5.1238

moderate.headline: Once a week, check in with someone you trust about what drained you and what nourished you.
moderate.how_to: Share one thing that drained you and one that gave you energy, focusing on how they made you feel. When they share, respond with interest.

evidence.summary: Research shows that sharing personal experiences, especially feelings, is a strong predictor of how close people feel during a conversation. A weekly check-in with someone you trust helps build that closeness.
evidence.detail_source: Laurenceau 1998 (emotional disclosure > factual; partner responsiveness).
references: Laurenceau, J.-P., Barrett, L. F., & Pietromonaco, P. R. (1998). Intimacy as an interpersonal process: The importance of self-disclosure, partner disclosure, and perceived partner responsiveness in interpersonal exchanges. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1238–1251. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.74.5.1238

deep.headline: Share one personal reflection with someone you trust every week.
deep.how_to: Pick a regular day and share something honest about how you've been feeling. Respond supportively when they share.

evidence.summary: Research shows that sharing personal feelings, more than facts alone, is a strong predictor of how close people feel. A regular personal reflection helps build trust and connection in your close relationships.
evidence.detail_source: Laurenceau 1998 (emotional disclosure > factual; partner responsiveness).
references: Laurenceau, J.-P., Barrett, L. F., & Pietromonaco, P. R. (1998). Intimacy as an interpersonal process: The importance of self-disclosure, partner disclosure, and perceived partner responsiveness in interpersonal exchanges. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(5), 1238–1251. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.74.5.1238

gentle.headline: Share tonight's sleep intention with someone: what you're going to try tonight.
gentle.how_to: Write it as an 'if-then' or 'when-then' plan, for example 'When it's 10pm, I'll put my phone on charge in the kitchen', and tell a partner, friend or family member.

evidence.summary: Research shows that making a specific plan for what you'll do helps people reach their goals. Sharing tonight's sleep plan with someone turns an idea into a clear commitment.
evidence.detail_source: Implementation intentions ('if-then' plans), Gollwitzer & Sheeran 2006 (not indexed in PubMed; checked against publisher record); Hennessy 2020.
references: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1

Hennessy, E. A., Johnson, B. T., Acabchuk, R. L., McCloskey, K., & Stewart-James, J. (2020). Self-regulation mechanisms in health behavior change: a systematic meta-review of meta-analyses, 2006-2017. Health Psychology Review, 14(1), 6–42. https://doi.org/10.1080/17437199.2019.1679654

moderate.headline: Share your sleep goal with someone and, if useful, tell them how it went.
moderate.how_to: Set a specific goal, for example 'In bed by 10:30pm on 5 nights weekly', and tell them. Afterwards, share how it went.

evidence.summary: Research shows that making specific plans helps people achieve their goals, and that self-regulation strategies such as goal setting and feedback can support behaviour change. Sharing your sleep goal and how it went helps you stay on track. A large umbrella review of digital health programmes also found strong evidence for social support, goal setting and feedback.
evidence.detail_source: Hennessy 2020 (goal setting, feedback, self-monitoring effective for some behaviours); Mair 2023 added (social support, goals and planning, feedback and monitoring).
references: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1

deep.headline: Once a week, check in with someone about what helped or hindered your sleep.
deep.how_to: Note one thing that helped and one that got in the way, and share them.

evidence.summary: Self-regulation research supports monitoring and reflecting on your progress as ways to change behaviour. A quick check-in with someone helps you learn what works best for your sleep. A large umbrella review of digital health programmes also found strong evidence for self-monitoring, feedback and social support.
evidence.detail_source: Hennessy 2020; Mair 2023 added (feedback and monitoring; social support).
references: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(06)38002-1

gentle.headline: Share one thing that helped your sleep weekly with someone.
gentle.how_to: Keep it specific, for example 'No coffee after 1pm helped me fall asleep faster.'

evidence.summary: Self-regulation techniques, such as tracking and reflecting on what works, are widely used to build healthier habits, though research on any single technique is mixed. Sharing a sleep win helps you remember what worked and passes the idea on to others. A large umbrella review of digital health programmes found strong evidence for social support and for feedback and monitoring.
evidence.detail_source: Mair 2023 added (as the Change Log recommended, since Spring 2021 found no single technique consistently effective).

moderate.headline: Share something you learned about your sleep with someone.
moderate.how_to: Think of a pattern you've noticed, for example 'I sleep worse after a late workout' or 'I wake up more easily when I'm in bed by 11pm', and share it in a sentence or two.

evidence.summary: Self-regulation techniques are widely used to build healthier habits, though research on any single technique is mixed. Sharing what you've learned about your sleep helps you reflect on it and may help them too. A large umbrella review of digital health programmes found strong evidence for social support and for feedback and monitoring.

deep.headline: Talk through a sleep reflection with someone when it feels useful.
deep.how_to: This could be about a change you've made, a setback or something you're still working on. Try answering three questions: What have I noticed? What's working? What will I try next?

evidence.summary: Reflection is a common self-regulation technique in health programmes, though research on any single technique is mixed. Talking a sleep reflection through with someone helps you build on what you learn. A large umbrella review of digital health programmes found strong evidence for social support and for feedback and monitoring.

gentle.headline: Congratulate someone on a sleep win weekly.
gentle.how_to: Think of a partner, friend or family member who has made progress, however small, and send a short, specific message, for example 'Great job keeping to your bedtime all week!'

evidence.summary: Research on digital health programmes identifies behaviour-change techniques that help people improve their health habits. Recognising a teammate's progress is a simple way to support each other along the way.
evidence.detail_source: Mair 2023 (social support). Message format = practical how-to.

Annals of Behavioral Medicine, 57(10), 817–835. https://doi.org/10.1093/abm/kaad041

moderate.headline: Celebrate sleep wins with others, big or small.
moderate.how_to: When you or someone close to you reaches a goal, mark it with a message or a small celebration.

evidence.summary: Research identifies behaviour-change techniques that work well in digital health programmes. Celebrating sleep wins together helps keep everyone's progress visible and motivating.
evidence.detail_source: Mair 2023 (social support; feedback).
references: Mair, J. L., Salamanca-Sanabria, A., Augsburger, M., Frese, B. F., Abend, S., Jakob, R., Kowatsch, T., & Haug, S. (2023). deep.headline: Team up with someone to keep up a sleep habit together.
deep.how_to: Agree on a shared habit, set a goal together, check in regularly and encourage each other.

evidence.summary: Research supports several behaviour-change techniques used in digital health programmes. Supporting each other is a practical way to put them to work and keep your sleep habits going.
evidence.detail_source: Mair 2023 (social support; goals and planning; feedback and monitoring).

gentle.headline: Call someone weekly who you would normally just text.
gentle.how_to: Pick a friend or family member and ring them for a short chat.

evidence.summary: Experiments found that conversations including voice, such as phone or video calls, created stronger social bonds than text-based ones, with no increase in awkwardness, but people wrongly expected calls to be more awkward. People also underestimate how much others want to connect.
evidence.detail_source: Kumar & Epley 2021 (voice > text for bonding); Epley & Schroeder 2014 (underestimating others' interest). Verified in PubMed.
references: Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2021). It's surprisingly nice to hear you: Misunderstanding the impact of communication media can lead to suboptimal choices of how to connect with others. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 150(3), 595–607. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000962
Epley, N., & Schroeder, J. (2014). Mistakenly seeking solitude. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(5), 1980–1999. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037323

moderate.headline: Replace texting with a phone or video call 2–3 times weekly.
moderate.how_to: Choose the conversations where you'd most like to feel close, such as catching up with an old friend.

evidence.summary: A field experiment found that reconnecting with an old friend by phone created a stronger bond than doing so by email, and laboratory studies found voice and video chats built stronger connection than text chat.
evidence.detail_source: Kumar & Epley 2021 (phone vs email reconnection). Verified in PubMed.
references: Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2021). It's surprisingly nice to hear you: Misunderstanding the impact of communication media can lead to suboptimal choices of how to connect with others. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 150(3), 595–607. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000962

deep.headline: Schedule regular phone or video calls with the people who matter to you, especially those who live far away.
deep.how_to: Set a recurring time, for example a weekly call with a parent or a monthly video catch-up with old friends.

evidence.summary: Experiments found that phone, video and voice chats consistently created stronger social bonds than text-based communication, without more awkwardness.
evidence.detail_source: Kumar & Epley 2021. Scheduling = practical how-to. Verified in PubMed.
references: Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2021). It's surprisingly nice to hear you: Misunderstanding the impact of communication media can lead to suboptimal choices of how to connect with others. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 150(3), 595–607. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000962

gentle.headline: Send a short message to someone you've lost touch with.
gentle.how_to: You don't need a special reason. A simple 'I was thinking of you' is enough.

evidence.summary: Research shows that many people hesitate to reach out to old friends, yet people underestimate how much others appreciate being contacted. A short message is an easy first step.
evidence.detail_source: Aknin & Sandstrom 2024; Liu 2023. (new practice added to complete the Gentle/Moderate/Deep family)
references: Aknin, L. B., & Sandstrom, G. M. (2024). People are surprisingly hesitant to reach out to old friends. Communications Psychology, 2(1), 34. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-024-00075-8

moderate.headline: Invite someone you've lost touch with to talk or meet.
moderate.how_to: Suggest a call, coffee or meal at a specific time. If it feels awkward, that's normal, and it usually passes once you start talking.

evidence.summary: Research shows that many people have lost touch with an old friend but hesitate to reach out, even when they think the friend would appreciate hearing from them. Sending an invitation is a small step that can bring back a meaningful connection. People also underestimate how much others appreciate being contacted, especially by someone less close. An intervention that eased people's worries about reaching out increased the number who did so by two-thirds.
evidence.detail_source: Aknin & Sandstrom 2024 (hesitancy; intervention easing anxiety ↑ reaching out by two-thirds); Liu 2023 added (underestimated appreciation).

deep.headline: Invite someone who might appreciate company to share a meal with you regularly, for example every week or fortnight.
deep.how_to: Think of someone who may be alone a lot, such as a neighbour or new colleague, and suggest a regular time and place.

evidence.summary: Research found that social connection matters for health, with isolation and loneliness each linked with a higher risk of early death. Research on shared eating links meals together with social connection, so an invitation is a meaningful way to connect. People also underestimate how much others appreciate being contacted, especially by someone less close.
evidence.detail_source: Holt-Lunstad 2015; Dunbar 2017; Liu 2023 added.

gentle.headline: List the groups you belong to, and pick one you'd like to be more involved in.
gentle.how_to: Groups can be anything you feel part of: a club, team, class, faith community, volunteering group or group of friends.

evidence.summary: A study of over 5,000 adults found that the number of social groups people belonged to strongly predicted later depression, with fewer groups predicting more depression.
evidence.detail_source: Cruwys 2013. Listing groups = preparatory step. Verified in PubMed.
references: Cruwys, T., Dingle, G. A., Haslam, C., Haslam, S. A., Jetten, J., & Morton, T. A. (2013). moderate.headline: Go to a meeting, session or event of a group weekly.
moderate.how_to: This could be a club, class, choir, community group or faith gathering.

evidence.summary: Research found that belonging to social groups protects against depression, and a study following new adult education classes found members grew closer over time, with singing groups bonding fastest.
evidence.detail_source: Cruwys 2013; Pearce 2015 (singing and non-singing classes over 7 months). Verified in PubMed.
references: Cruwys, T., Dingle, G. A., Haslam, C., Haslam, S. A., Jetten, J., & Morton, T. A. (2013). deep.headline: Join a new group and attend regularly, aiming to belong to more than one group.
deep.how_to: Choose a group that meets regularly and commit to going for several months.

evidence.summary: A study of over 5,000 adults found that group memberships protected against future depression; among depressed people with no groups, joining one group reduced the risk of relapse by 24% and joining three by 63%.
evidence.detail_source: Cruwys 2013 (1 group −24%, 3 groups −63% relapse risk). Verified in PubMed.
references: Cruwys, T., Dingle, G. A., Haslam, C., Haslam, S. A., Jetten, J., & Morton, T. A. (2013). gentle.headline: Give a hug to someone close to you today, if they welcome it.
gentle.how_to: Ask first if you're not sure.

evidence.summary: A study of 404 healthy adults found that more frequent hugs helped buffer the effects of interpersonal stress and were linked with less severe illness when infected with a cold virus.
evidence.detail_source: Cohen 2015 (daily hugs over 14 days; observational). Consent note = precaution. Verified in PubMed.
references: Cohen, S., Janicki-Deverts, D., Turner, R. B., & Doyle, W. J. (2015). Does hugging provide stress-buffering social support? A study of susceptibility to upper respiratory infection and illness. Psychological Science, 26(2), 135–147. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797614559284

moderate.headline: Share a hug or other affectionate touch with someone close to you on most days.
moderate.how_to: This could be a hug, holding hands or an arm around a shoulder, whatever feels comfortable for both of you.

evidence.summary: A meta-analysis of 137 studies found that touch interventions reduced pain, depression and anxiety in adults, with touch from a familiar person as beneficial as from a health professional; a separate study linked frequent hugs with protection against stress.
evidence.detail_source: Packheiser 2024; Cohen 2015. Verified in PubMed.
references: Packheiser, J., Hartmann, H., Fredriksen, K., Gazzola, V., Keysers, C., & Michon, F. (2024). deep.headline: Build daily affectionate touch into your close relationships.
deep.how_to: Talk with your partner, family or close friends about the kinds of touch you each enjoy, such as a morning hug or a hand massage, and make it part of your day.

evidence.summary: A meta-analysis of 137 studies found that touch reduced depression and anxiety in adults, that touch from a familiar person was as beneficial as from a professional, and that human touch had greater mental health benefits than touch from objects or robots.
evidence.detail_source: Packheiser 2024. Consent conversation = practical how-to. Verified in PubMed.
references: Packheiser, J., Hartmann, H., Fredriksen, K., Gazzola, V., Keysers, C., & Michon, F. (2024). A systematic review and multivariate meta-analysis of the physical and mental health benefits of touch interventions. Nature Human Behaviour, 8(6), 1088–1107. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-024-01841-8

gentle.headline: Today, start one brief conversation with someone you don't know well (e.g., a neighbour, barista or colleague).
gentle.how_to: Keep it simple: ask how their day is going or comment on something you share.

evidence.summary: Research shows that chatting with acquaintances, not just close friends and family, is linked with feeling happier and more connected that day. A brief conversation with a neighbour, barista or colleague can brighten your day.
evidence.detail_source: Sandstrom & Dunn 2014 (more interactions with weak ties → more happiness and belonging that day).
references: Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167214529799

moderate.headline: Weekly, start a brief conversation with three different people you know a little, but not well.
moderate.how_to: Think of people you see regularly but rarely talk to, and use an easy opener.

evidence.summary: Research shows that interacting with acquaintances is linked with greater happiness and a stronger sense of belonging on the same day. A few brief conversations across the week help you feel more connected.
evidence.detail_source: Sandstrom & Dunn 2014 (more interactions with weak ties → more happiness and belonging that day).
references: Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167214529799

deep.headline: Each day, take one opportunity to start a brief conversation with someone you don't know well.
deep.how_to: Look for everyday moments, such as queues or waiting for a meeting, and ask an open question.

evidence.summary: Research shows that interacting with people you don't know well is linked with greater happiness and a stronger sense of belonging that day. A daily conversation helps you feel more at home in your community.
evidence.detail_source: Sandstrom & Dunn 2014 (more interactions with weak ties → more happiness and belonging that day).
references: Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167214529799

gentle.headline: When you buy food or coffee weekly, have a brief friendly chat with the person serving you.
gentle.how_to: Ask how their day is going or comment on something you share.

evidence.summary: Research shows that interacting with people you don't know well is linked with greater happiness and a stronger sense of belonging on the same day.
evidence.detail_source: Sandstrom & Dunn 2014. (new practice added to complete the Gentle/Moderate/Deep family)
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167214529799

moderate.headline: Sit with someone you don't know well at a shared lunch or break weekly.
moderate.how_to: For example, join a colleague from another team in the canteen or a neighbour at a community event.

evidence.summary: Research shows that interacting with people you don't know well is linked with greater happiness and belonging, and people who eat with others more often report greater wellbeing.
evidence.detail_source: Sandstrom & Dunn 2014; Dunbar 2017. (new practice added to complete the Gentle/Moderate/Deep family)
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167214529799

deep.headline: Invite someone you do not know well to share a meal or coffee.
deep.how_to: This could be a newer colleague, a neighbour or someone from a class. Keep it low-pressure.

evidence.summary: Research shows that interacting with people you don't know well, not just close friends and family, is linked with greater happiness and a stronger sense of belonging. Sharing a meal or coffee is an easy way to build these connections.
evidence.detail_source: Sandstrom & Dunn 2014; Dunbar 2017.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167214529799

gentle.headline: Share one meal weekly with a friend, family member or colleague.
gentle.how_to: Any meal counts: a family dinner, lunch with a colleague or breakfast with a friend.

evidence.summary: Research shows that people who eat with others more often report greater happiness, life satisfaction and trust, and feel more engaged with their community. Sharing a meal is one of the simplest ways to connect.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017; Holt-Lunstad 2010.
references: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

moderate.headline: Invite someone to lunch or dinner and share the meal together weekly.
moderate.how_to: Choose a friend, neighbour, family member or colleague and suggest a specific day, for example 'Are you free for lunch on Thursday?'

evidence.summary: Research shows that people who eat with others more often report greater happiness, life satisfaction and trust. Inviting someone to share a meal turns food into connection.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017. Invitation format = practical how-to.

Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

deep.headline: Host a shared meal and invite people you care about to contribute if they would like to.
deep.how_to: Pick a date and invite a few people. Asking each person to bring a dish keeps it simple.

evidence.summary: Research shows that shared meals with more people are linked with feeling closer to those you eat with. Hosting a meal is a warm way to bring people together.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017 (more people → closer). Pot-luck = practical how-to.
references: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316

gentle.headline: Share a healthy recipe with a friend or family member and, if you both want to, try it together.
gentle.how_to: Choose a recipe with plenty of vegetables, legumes or whole grains.

evidence.summary: Evidence from many studies found that learning what others eat influences both how much and which foods people choose. Sharing a healthy recipe with others can inspire healthier choices for you both.
evidence.detail_source: Robinson 2014 norms (informational eating norms influence choice and intake); Dunbar 2017.

moderate.headline: Cook a recipe a friend or family member shared with you, and tell them how it turned out.
moderate.how_to: Afterwards, thank them and tell them what you enjoyed.

evidence.summary: Research shows that feeling grateful for everyday kindnesses predicts stronger relationships in the following weeks, and that the food choices of those around us shape our own. deep.headline: Invite a friend or family member to cook a meal with you.
deep.how_to: Suggest cooking together at your home or theirs, and share the tasks.

evidence.summary: Research shows that people who eat together more often have more friends they can rely on for support. Cooking a meal with someone is a natural way to build that kind of connection.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017.
references: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316

gentle.headline: At one shared meal weekly, mention something that made you laugh recently.
gentle.how_to: Think of it beforehand so it's ready.

evidence.summary: Research shows that shared meals with more laughter are linked with feeling closer to the people you eat with. Sharing something funny is an easy way to start.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017. (new practice added to complete the Gentle/Moderate/Deep family)
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

moderate.headline: During one shared meal weekly, share a memory or story from the past.
moderate.how_to: Think of one beforehand so it's ready.

evidence.summary: Research shows that shared meals with more laughter and reminiscing are linked with feeling closer to the people you eat with. Sharing a story or a funny moment helps make an ordinary meal memorable.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017 (laughter and reminiscing).
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

deep.headline: During one shared meal weekly, invite everyone at the table to share a favourite memory or a story that still makes them laugh.
deep.how_to: Ask an easy, open question and go first to get things started.

evidence.summary: Research shows that shared meals with more laughter and reminiscing are linked with feeling closer to the people you eat with. Inviting everyone to share a story helps everyone at the table feel connected.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

gentle.headline: After a shared meal, tell someone one thing you appreciated about it.
gentle.how_to: Say it before you leave or send a message later, and be specific.

moderate.how_to: Be specific about the food, the effort or the company.

deep.headline: Write a thank-you letter to someone who often cooks for or eats with you, and give it to them.
deep.how_to: Say specifically what the meals and their company have meant to you.

gentle.headline: Share a memory about a meal or recipe that has special meaning to you.
gentle.how_to: Tell someone about it over a meal or in a message.

evidence.summary: Research shows that shared meals with more reminiscing are linked with greater closeness among the people present. Sharing a meaningful food memory is a gentle way to connect.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

moderate.headline: Cook a dish linked to a special food memory, and share the story with whoever eats it with you.
moderate.how_to: Choose a recipe tied to a person, place or time in your life.

evidence.summary: Research shows that shared meals with more reminiscing are linked with greater closeness among the people present. Cooking a meaningful dish and sharing its story brings this into a meal.
evidence.detail_source: Dunbar 2017. (new practice added to complete the Gentle/Moderate/Deep family)

deep.headline: Cook a family recipe with someone from a younger generation.
deep.how_to: Choose a dish that matters to your family, give them hands-on jobs, and share the story behind it as you cook.

evidence.summary: Research shows that people who eat with others more often report greater happiness, trust and social support. A review of 50 years of research also links family routines and rituals with stronger family relationships and better child adjustment.
evidence.detail_source: Fiese 2002; Dunbar 2017.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4

gentle.headline: At one meal weekly, do a small ritual before eating, such as a toast or a moment of thanks.
gentle.how_to: Do it yourself rather than just watching, and pause briefly before you start eating.

evidence.summary: Research found that performing a small ritual before eating increases how much people enjoy and value their food, especially when they perform it themselves.

moderate.headline: Create one meal weekly that feels worth celebrating, with a small ritual before you eat.
moderate.how_to: Before eating, do a short ritual yourself, such as setting the table in a particular way or raising a toast, then pause briefly before you start.

evidence.summary: Research found that performing a small ritual before eating increases how much people enjoy and value their food, even with ordinary foods. Making a meal feel special helps you savour it more.
evidence.detail_source: Vohs 2013 (ritual performed personally; short delay heightens enjoyment).

deep.headline: Create a weekly ritual meal with the people you live with or care about, on the same day each week.
deep.how_to: Keep the same small rituals each time, such as a toast or everyone sharing one good thing from their week.
